newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Oct int'l trade gap $7.99 bln.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. Oct int'l trade gap $7.99 bln.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported the October international trade deficit at $7.99 billion against a revised $11.44 billion gap the prior month. Experts had expected a gap of $10.4 billion in October.
PETER KRETZMER, ECONOMIST, NATIONSBANC CAPITAL MARKETS
INC: "Obviously a much bigger narrowing than we expected. It was a good sign for the economy that exports were up 4.2 percent."

Kretzmer added: "The initial effect is it adds to fourth quarter growth. It certainly is the kind of number that puts my Gross Domestic Product growth estimate above 2.0 percent rather than below 2.0 percent for the quarter.
"The dollar is strong already, but the market reaction today to this data should be greater dollar strrength. In terms of this deficit, the dollar's strength is not hurting dollar exports too badly."

ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND AN ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "The trade deficit definitely was much narrower and it points to stronger growth, suggesting maybe up 2.5 to 3.0 percent growth with exports leading the way. (This means) a good economy ... it supports the view that the economy is stronger going into 1997."
JOHN RYDING, MANAGING DIRECTOR AND SENIOR ECONOMIST, BEAR STEARNS & CO INC: "This is a very surprising narrowing of the trade gap.
"It implies that GDP growth could receive a significant positive contribution from trade for the fourth quarter. It could add 1/2 to 1.0 percent to GDP, a sizable amount," Ryding added.

DAVID SLOAN, SENIOR ECONOMIST, I.D.E.A. INC: "The deficit fell more than most people had expected. We were quite optimistic (with a forecast of) $9.8 billion, and it was quite a bit narrower than that. The aircraft exports are up about $1.0 billion. That was a special factor. There aren't that many other special factors.
"Auto exports and imports were both depressed by the (General Motors Corp) strike in Canada.

Discussing the trade gap with Japan, which rose 30.9 percent to $4.96 billion, Sloan added: "That was partly a seasonal factor. The figures for Japan are not seasonally adjusted and they always widen in October because of the new model year in autos."
